chapter_theme: Under the heading நன்றியில் செல்வம், fourteen verses on wealth that does no good: ill-gotten gain that perishes as it seems to grow, wealth in weak hands that draws attack, the hoard neither given nor enjoyed, the miser's piety and his lost next birth, giving that passes over kin, the feigned kindness and the false plea of poverty, the honest refusal set against killing hope, and the gift wasted on the ungrateful.

213.reading: The verse asks whether those who walk the good way would covet the rare wealth gained by those who walk the wrong way, and answers with the proverb that evil things perish even as they seem to prosper.
213.nuance: The address to the lord of the shore, where the loud water seems to rush in, mirrors the proverb: the wave's advance looks like gain and is followed by its ebb. The ill-gotten fortune is not denied; it is said to be the look of growth that precedes ruin.

pazhamozhi.literal: evil things perish in the very act of seeming to thrive

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the type of man who grows rich by wrong ways

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the good do not desire wealth won by wrong means, since its rise is the shape of its fall

214.reading: The verse says that when men who lack any resolve proven over time come into wealth of real worth, it is like the mango tree that bears fruit and so draws the throwing-stick upon itself.
214.nuance: The wealth itself is not blamed: it is called fine (நன்மையின் மாண்ட). The fault is in the holder, who has no tested firmness to guard it, so his gain becomes the reason he is struck. தொன்மையின் மாண்ட துணிவு may mean resolve made excellent by long use or by ancestry; the line does not settle which.

pazhamozhi.literal: the mango that fruits takes the cudgel upon itself

story.act: no story; a fruiting mango is pelted by those who want its fruit

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth in weak hands draws attack on its owner

215.reading: The verse says those who, even having wealth, neither give to others nor enjoy it themselves, and whose kin also cling and grow tight, are named by the proverb of unwashed hair beside the lopping of trees.
215.nuance: Line 2 may say that the miser's kin, holding on to him, become tight-fisted in turn, or that they cling to the hoard. The proverb மரங்குறைப்ப மண்ணா மயிர் is obscure: one reading is that they labour at felling trees while their own hair stays unwashed, toil without any enjoyment, which fits தாந்துவ்வார் (they do not enjoy). The image is not certain.

pazhamozhi.literal: they lop trees, and their hair stays unwashed

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the hoarder who neither gives nor enjoys

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth neither given nor enjoyed is labour without fruit, and the habit spreads to the kin

216.reading: The verse says that the drum-proclaimed wealth gained by a man who knows neither how to give nor how to enjoy is a dog's coconut.
216.nuance: A dog may own a coconut but cannot break it open or eat it: the proverb is about possession without access. The booming drum (முழங்கு முரசு) marks royal or lordly wealth, so the verse aims at a ruler or great man, not a small householder.
216.domain_note: a lord whose wealth is proclaimed by the drum

pazhamozhi.literal: a coconut that a dog has got

story.act: no story; a dog guarding a coconut it cannot open

pazhamozhi.applied_to: great wealth held by one who cannot give or enjoy it is possessed and useless

217.reading: The verse says that the wealth of one who, though he has seen rulers of the whole sea-girt earth fall and vanish like a dance in a festival town, still gives nothing because giving feels like loss, is the loss of the eye together with its beauty.
217.nuance: The miser calls giving இழவு, loss; the proverb turns his word back on him, since his hoard is the real இழவு, and a double one, as losing an eye destroys sight and looks at once. The kings who vanished like a festival dance make the argument from impermanence: wealth will go in any case.

pazhamozhi.literal: losing the eye together with its beauty

story.act: no story; the loss of an eye, which costs both use and looks

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the hoard of one who will not give is a double loss, of use and of honour

218.reading: The verse asks what it matters whether those who, knowing the want of those who beg aloud, wrap up their own goods tightly, fear evil deeds or not, and answers with the proverb: what matter whether a blind eye sleeps or wakes?
218.nuance: The target is the miser who claims piety: his fear of தீவினை is like the blindness of an eye, the same whether shut or open, because it changes nothing he does. மாவினை may be his goods or provisions (மா, grain or flour) and பொதிகிற்பார் those who bundle them away; the exact object is uncertain.

pazhamozhi.literal: what if a blind eye sleeps, what if it does not

story.act: no story; a blind eye open or closed sees alike

pazhamozhi.applied_to: fear of sin that does not move a man to give is no different from having none

219.reading: The verse says that those who give nothing toward the birth that follows and, by the attachment that pursues them, keep their wealth and die, are those who in the pressing hour leave the guts behind and send off the outer fence.
219.nuance: The proverb குடரொழிய மீவேலி போக்குபவர் is obscure. On one reading it sets the inner thing (the gut, what life depends on) against the outer fence, so the hoarder guards the outside and loses the inside: his wealth stays, his next birth goes unprovided. படரும் பிறப்பு, the birth that spreads onward, makes giving a provision for the coming life.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who, the gut being lost, send off the upper fence

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the hoarder who dies with his wealth

pazhamozhi.applied_to: keeping wealth till death and giving nothing for the next birth protects the outer while the inner is lost

220.reading: The verse says that failing to relieve the gnawing hunger of those who come with love and of one's own kin, while helping strangers, is wholly like the black palmyra.
220.nuance: வம்பர் may be strangers or idle, worthless men; either way they are set against kin and those who came in love. The proverb's image is only கரும்பனை, the dark palmyra, and the verse does not say how it applies; on one reading the tall palm gives nothing to what stands at its foot. The opening quotation mark falls before ஆற்ற, so the proverb includes that word.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is wholly of the nature of the black palmyra

story.act: no story; the palmyra stands for help that does not reach those nearest

pazhamozhi.applied_to: giving that passes over hungry kin to reach strangers is misdirected

221.reading: The verse describes men who do not give, have no strength, are harsh of speech and do not help one who has toiled when trouble comes, says that gaining wealth from them is no better than losing it, and calls leaving them leaving behind the stack of an old field.
221.nuance: Line 3 is hard: இழந்ததில் செல்வம் பெறுதலும் இன்னார் may say that what one gets from such men is as good as lost, or that they are men from whom no wealth comes. The proverb then counsels quitting them, as one leaves an old field's threshed stack with nothing lost.

pazhamozhi.literal: leaving behind the straw stack of an old field

story.act: no story; abandoning a stack already threshed, from which nothing more comes

pazhamozhi.applied_to: to leave the ungiving is to lose nothing

222.reading: The verse says that when the destitute, unable to bear it, have spoken so that their need is understood, to make a show of doing good and then dash their hope by a hard act is to tie the mouthful of grass to a beast's neck and let it go.
222.nuance: The beast with grass tied at its neck has its food beside its mouth and cannot eat it: the image is of a gift shown and withheld, worse than a refusal. நசையழுங்க, hope crushed, is the same phrase Naladiyar 111 uses of one who keeps the asker waiting.

pazhamozhi.literal: tying that mouthful of grass on the neck and letting it go

story.act: no story; a beast turned loose with its grass bound to its neck

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a feigned kindness that kills the asker's hope torments rather than helps

223.reading: The verse says that if one who could help, asked by those long close to him, pleads that he has nothing, it is the tree a herdsman has cut.
223.nuance: The refusal is aimed at old intimates (அடையப் பயின்றார்), not strangers. The herdsman's tree is hacked for leaves to feed his flock and left standing but maimed; on that reading the bond is not cut through but spoiled. ஆற்றுவரா may also read as those askers who could not bear it; the proverb's application is uncertain.

pazhamozhi.literal: a tree hacked by a herdsman

story.act: no story; a tree lopped by a herdsman for his flock

pazhamozhi.applied_to: pleading poverty to old friends maims the bond without ending it

224.reading: The verse says that those who stand and beg before men whose minds are hard as wood get nothing, as one gets nothing by seeking alms inside a monastery.
224.nuance: The பள்ளி is a house of renouncers, who themselves live on alms: to beg there is to beg from beggars. The proverb makes the hard-hearted rich man equal in yield to one who owns nothing.

pazhamozhi.literal: entering a monastery to ask for alms

story.act: no story; begging alms where the dwellers themselves beg

pazhamozhi.applied_to: asking of the hard-hearted rich yields as little as asking of those who own nothing

225.reading: The verse says that giving what one can and saying 'I have none' are both no disgrace but the way of the world; but if, while one who has come in hope stands waiting, a man does not share and eat, there is no world for him who killed that hope.
225.nuance: Its first two lines are almost word for word the opening of Naladiyar 111; the two verses part only in the proverb. The fault is not refusal but keeping the asker standing (நிற்ப) and then not sharing. செல்லுலகம் இல் denies him a world to go to after death.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no world to go to for one who killed hope

story.act: no story; the proverb names the hope-killer as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an honest refusal is no fault, but to hold the asker in hope and then deny him forfeits the next world

226.reading: The verse says such men will not, when need comes through their kin or themselves, do anything and stand as equals, and that all that is given to those who do not rejoice in what was done for them is lost.
226.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are elliptic: they seem to describe men who neither help nor return help in trouble, as if to say what kind of recipient wastes a gift. The proverb judges the gift by the receiver's gladness, not by any return.

pazhamozhi.literal: all that is given to those who do not rejoice is loss

story.act: no story; the ungrateful recipient as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a gift to one who takes no joy in kindness is wasted

links.note: Kural 113 bids one let go at once any gain that comes from leaving fairness, even if it brings good; Pazhamozhi 213 says the good do not even desire such gain, and gives the reason in the proverb.
links.teaches: The Kural's command assumes the unfair gain may truly bring good; the proverb denies even that, so renouncing it becomes good sense rather than sacrifice.
links.list_adds: its proverb and the image of the onrushing wave add a mechanism, that the gain's apparent growth is the first stage of its loss, which the couplet leaves out.

links.note: Kural 659 says what is taken with tears goes with tears; Pazhamozhi 213 says evil gains perish as they seem to thrive.
links.teaches: Together the two make ill-gotten wealth self-cancelling twice over: it leaves the way it came, and its swelling is the very shape of the leaving.
links.list_adds: it sets the claim as a choice the good make in advance, refusing to want such wealth, where the couplet only forecasts its end.

links.note: Kural 1008 likens the wealth of the unloved to a poison tree fruiting in the middle of town; Pazhamozhi 214 likens the wealth of the irresolute to a mango that fruits and draws the stick.
links.teaches: The same fruiting tree cuts two ways: in the Kural the fruit is useless to the town, in Pazhamozhi it is coveted and brings blows on the tree, so wealth harms either its neighbours or its holder.
links.list_adds: it moves the fault from the owner's being unloved to his lacking tested resolve, and turns the tree from an emblem of uselessness into a target.

links.note: Kural 1009 says others take the wealth gathered by giving up love and virtue; Pazhamozhi 214 says wealth draws attackers when its holder lacks firmness, though the wealth itself is good.
links.teaches: Losing wealth to others has two causes in the pair: a vice in how it was gathered and a weakness in who holds it, so even rightly gained wealth is not safe in weak hands.
links.list_adds: it adds a condition the couplet lacks, that the wealth may be நன்மையின் மாண்ட and still be lost, because the danger lies in the owner's want of resolve.

links.note: Naladiyar 278 says the miser's heirs do not give once the wealth is theirs; Pazhamozhi 215 says that the miser's kin too cling and grow tight while he lives.
links.teaches: Read together, miserliness is shown as a household trait passed sideways to kin in life and down to heirs after death, not a private vice.
links.list_adds: it pairs not giving with not enjoying and sets the kin's clinging in the same breath, so the hoard is shown corrupting the whole circle around it.

links.note: Kural 1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores; Pazhamozhi 216 says the drum-proclaimed wealth of such a man is a dog's coconut.
links.teaches: The Kural says he has nothing; the proverb sharpens this to having something he cannot open, so the miser is not poor but locked out of his own possession.
links.list_adds: its proverb replaces the couplet's abstract 'nothing' with an image of possession without access, and the drum carries the claim to royal wealth.

links.note: Naladiyar 9 says the man who only guards his wealth without using or giving it will be thought of as one who has lost it; Pazhamozhi 217 says the non-giver's wealth is a loss like losing an eye with its beauty.
links.teaches: Both verses answer the miser's fear of loss by calling his keeping the real loss, and the proverb adds that it is a double loss of use and of looks.
links.list_adds: it grounds the claim in the fall of rulers of the whole earth, an argument from impermanence the quatrain does not make, and turns the miser's own word இழவு against him.

links.note: Kural 1007 likens the non-giver's wealth to a beautiful woman growing old alone; Pazhamozhi 217 likens it to losing the eye together with its beauty.
links.teaches: Both images make unused wealth a beauty wasted, but the Kural's beauty fades unseen while Pazhamozhi's is destroyed with the organ, so one is waste by neglect and the other by injury.
links.list_adds: its proverb replaces slow fading with sudden destruction, matching its frame of kings who vanished like a festival dance.

links.note: Kural 228 asks whether the hard-eyed hoarders do not know the joy of giving; Pazhamozhi 218 says whether such hoarders fear sin or not makes no difference.
links.teaches: The pair close the hoarder's two exits: he lacks the joy of giving, and his fear of sin, which might have stood in for it, counts for nothing without the act.
links.list_adds: its proverb of the blind eye, the same shut or open, rules out piety without giving, a point the couplet's appeal to pleasure does not reach.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 218 says the miser's fear of sin is idle; 219 says that those who give nothing toward the next birth keep their wealth and die.
links.teaches: The second verse supplies the consequence the first only implies: a fear of sin that does not give leaves the next birth unprovided.

links.note: Kural 1002 says the delusion of clinging without giving brings a மாணாப் பிறப்பு; Pazhamozhi 219 says those who give nothing for the coming birth hoard by attachment and die.
links.teaches: The Kural names the bad birth as the fruit of hoarding; Pazhamozhi makes giving the provision for that birth, so not giving is a failure to pack for a journey.
links.list_adds: it frames giving as something owed to the birth that follows (படரும் பிறப்பு) and names the attachment (பற்று) that holds the wealth, and its proverb sets outer guarding against inner loss.

links.note: Naladiyar 273 says the fool who hoards and dies is mocked by his own stored wealth; Pazhamozhi 219 says those who keep their wealth and die guard the outer fence while the inner is lost.
links.teaches: The two verses use the same phrase of keeping and dying and give the hoarder two judges, his wealth's mockery and his own lost next birth.
links.list_adds: it adds the next birth as the thing lost, where the quatrain stops at the mockery of the wealth that outlived him.

links.note: Naladiyar 269 likens the giving of fools to rain poured into the sea while the paddy withers; Pazhamozhi 220 says leaving the hunger of kin and lovers unrelieved while helping strangers is like the black palmyra.
links.teaches: Both make misdirected giving a vice, not a virtue: the Naladiyar faults giving where there is no need, Pazhamozhi names the need passed over, the hunger of one's own kin.
links.list_adds: it names who is passed over, those who came with love and one's kin, where the quatrain gives only the image of the parched field.

links.note: Naladiyar 261 says no one counts on the wealth of the worthless, as bats shun the cracked wood-apple; Pazhamozhi 221 lists the faults of the ungiving and calls leaving them leaving an old field's stack.
links.teaches: The quatrain says people do not approach such wealth; Pazhamozhi adds a counsel, that walking away costs nothing, so shunning the miser becomes a choice, not an instinct.
links.list_adds: it lists the miser's faults side by side (no giving, no strength, harsh speech, no help in trouble), making stinginess one of a cluster of failures.

links.note: Iniyavai Narpathu 26 names as sweet the worth of not killing the hope of those who come in desire; Pazhamozhi 222 shows the hope-killer at work, feigning kindness and then withholding.
links.teaches: The counted verse names the virtue bare; Pazhamozhi shows its opposite as a staged deceit, the gift dangled like grass tied at a beast's neck.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 222 shows a man who seems about to help and then dashes the asker's hope; 225 says an honest refusal is no fault but that killing hope forfeits the next world.
links.teaches: Read together, the pair say the wrong is not in refusing but in raising hope and then crushing it, and 225 names the price of what 222 depicts.

links.note: Kural 223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing', and giving, belong to the well-born; Pazhamozhi 223 condemns pleading 'nothing' to those long close when one could help.
links.teaches: The Kural measures the plea of poverty against birth; Pazhamozhi measures it against an old bond, so the same words are a fault of lineage in one and a wound to friendship in the other.
links.list_adds: it adds who is asking, old intimates, and its proverb of the hacked tree says what the false plea does to the bond, which the couplet does not consider.

links.note: Kural 1067 begs all beggars not to beg of those who conceal; Pazhamozhi 224 says those who beg of hard-minded men get nothing, like seeking alms in a monastery.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the warning; Pazhamozhi gives the reason in an image, that the hard rich man yields no more than renouncers who own nothing.
links.list_adds: its proverb equates the hard-hearted rich with those who themselves live on alms, a comparison the couplet does not draw.

links.note: Naladiyar 279 says the base yield only when strong men press them, like a cow milked by force; Pazhamozhi 224 says those who stand and beg before the hard-minded get nothing.
links.teaches: Read together, the hard-hearted are moved by force but never by entreaty, so the beggar's mode of asking is the one sure to fail.
links.list_adds: it fixes the asker's posture, standing before them (முன்னின்று இரந்தார்), as the thing that yields nothing, where the quatrain sets yielding gladly against yielding under force.

links.note: Naladiyar 111 opens with nearly the same two lines as Pazhamozhi 225: refusing what one cannot give is no disgrace and the way of the world; it then says keeping the asker waiting till hope dies is worse than killing gratitude, where Pazhamozhi says the hope-killer has no world to go to.
links.teaches: The shared lines show one maxim closed two ways, measured against ingratitude in the Naladiyar and against the next world in Pazhamozhi, so the same fault is given a moral rank and a cosmic penalty.
links.list_adds: the two verses share their first lines; what Pazhamozhi adds is its proverb, which turns the Naladiyar's comparison of faults into a sentence on the hope-killer's afterlife.

links.note: Purananuru 196, a bard to the Pandya Nanmaran, says that saying yes to what one can and no to what one cannot are both proper ways of a giver's friendship, while false promises and false refusals wound the asker and lessen the giver's fame.
links.teaches: The bard's complaint to a king and the ethics verse state the same rule about refusal, which shows the norm of the honest 'no' is older than the ethics works and was first argued from a suppliant's side.

links.note: Kural 1070 says the asker's life goes out at the word of refusal; Pazhamozhi 225 says refusing what one cannot give is no disgrace, and that the fault lies in keeping the asker in hope and then not sharing.
links.teaches: The Kural weighs every refusal by the asker's death of spirit; Pazhamozhi exempts the honest refusal and reserves the blame for the one who holds out hope and withholds.
links.list_adds: it divides refusal into the honest 'I have none' and the hope kept alive and killed, a distinction the couplet, which condemns concealment as such, does not make.

links.note: Kural 224 says being begged from is painful until one sees the asker's glad face; Pazhamozhi 226 says all that is given to those who do not rejoice in what was done is lost.
links.teaches: The pair make the receiver's gladness the completion of the gift: the Kural says it ends the giver's pain, Pazhamozhi that without it the gift itself is wasted.
links.list_adds: it turns the couplet's psychology of the giver into a judgement on the recipient, setting the ungrateful who will not stand by one in need as the wasted object of giving.

links.note: Naladiyar 98 says to give to those who cannot repay is duty and giving to those who repay is only a loan; Pazhamozhi 226 says giving to those who do not rejoice in kindness is all loss.
links.teaches: Together they say what a gift may and may not ask in return: no repayment, but gladness, so a recipient who cannot repay is fit and one who will not rejoice is not.
links.list_adds: it adds a condition the quatrain lacks, the recipient's joy in the kindness, without retracting its rule against seeking return.

source_issues: 222 line 3-4: the proverb has a closing quotation mark but no opening one; the proverb is taken to begin at அவ்வாயுறைப்.
220 lines 3-4: the opening quotation mark stands before ஆற்றக், so the adverb is inside the proverb as printed.
226 line 3: the opening quotation mark falls after செய்தது, so செய்தது is outside the proverb though it belongs to its clause.

215 line 4, 219 lines 3-4, 221 line 3, 223 line 4: the proverbs and phrases மரங்குறைப்ப மண்ணா மயிர், குடரொழிய மீவேலி, இழந்ததில் செல்வம் பெறுதலும் இன்னார், இடையன் எறிந்த மரம் are obscure and their application is uncertain.
225 lines 1-2 are nearly identical to Naladiyar 111 lines 1-2.
